m: Om. I take refuge in the body of Ardhanarishvara, like the flower of the bandhuka and like gold, bearing a beautiful rosary, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of the boon with the staffs of his own arms, adorned with the crescent moon, three-eyed.
Om. The king said:
Blessed one, what you have told me is wonderful: the glory of the Goddess's deed, resting on the slaying of Raktabija.
I wish to hear further what Shumbha did, and what the exceedingly angry Nishumbha did, when Raktabija had been struck down.
The seer said:
When Raktabija had been struck down, and when the others had been slain in battle, the asura Shumbha and Nishumbha became angry beyond measure.
Seeing the great army being destroyed, and bearing indignation, Nishumbha then rushed forward with the chief asura army.
In front of him, behind him, and on both sides, great asuras came to kill the Goddess, angry, biting their lips.
Shumbha too, of great valour, came surrounded by his own forces, angry, to slay Chandika, after fighting the mothers.
Then there was a very great battle between the Goddess and Shumbha and Nishumbha, a very fierce shower of arrows, like two clouds raining.
Chandika cut those arrows of the two of them with her own masses of arrows, and she struck the two lords of the asuras on their limbs with floods of weapons.
Nishumbha, taking a sharpened sword and a brightly shining shield, struck the lion, the Goddess's excellent mount, on the head.
When her mount was struck, the Goddess quickly cut Nishumbha's excellent sword with a razor-arrow, and also his shield marked with eight moons.
When shield and sword were cut, that asura hurled a spear. She split that too in two with her discus as it came toward her.
Then Nishumbha, the danava, swollen with anger, seized a trident. As it came, the Goddess crushed that too with a blow of her fist.
He then took up a mace and hurled it at Chandika. That too, split by the Goddess's trident, was reduced to ashes.
Then, as that bull among daityas came with an axe in his hand, the Goddess struck him with a flood of arrows and felled him to the ground.
When Nishumbha of terrible valour had fallen to the earth, his brother, exceedingly enraged, went forth to kill Ambika.
Standing in his chariot, very high, with excellent weapons grasped, he filled the whole sky with his eight unequalled arms, and he shone.
Seeing him coming, the Goddess sounded her conch, and she also made the twang of her bow exceedingly hard to bear.
She filled the quarters with the sound of her own bell, a sound that destroyed the splendour of the entire daitya army.
Then the lion, with great roars that drove away the great rut of elephants, filled the sky, the earth, and the ten directions.
Then Kali leapt up and struck the sky and the earth with her two hands. By that sound the earlier sounds were swallowed up.
Shivaduti gave an inauspicious loud laugh. The asuras trembled at those sounds, and Shumbha went into extreme anger.
When Ambika called out, Stand, stand, evil-minded one, the gods standing in the sky answered, Victory.
The spear that Shumbha released as he came, terrible with flame, looking like a peak of fire as it approached, was driven back by a great meteor.
The lion's roar filled the space of the three worlds. A dreadful thunderclap conquered it, O lord of the earth.
The Goddess cut the arrows released by Shumbha, and Shumbha cut the arrows she had sent, with his own fierce arrows, by the hundred and by the thousand.
Then Chandika, angry, struck him with her spear. Struck by her, he fell to the earth, unconscious.
Then Nishumbha, regaining consciousness and taking up his bow, struck the Goddess, Kali, and the lion with arrows.
The lord of the danavas, making ten thousand arms again, the son of Diti, covered Chandika with the discus weapon.
Then the blessed Durga, destroyer of the distress of difficult passage, the Goddess, cut those discs and those arrows with her own arrows.
Then Nishumbha, with speed, taking a mace, rushed at Chandika to kill her, surrounded by the daitya army.
As he came on, Chandika quickly cut the mace with a sharp-edged sword, and he took up a trident.
As Nishumbha, tormentor of the immortals, came with the trident in his hand, Chandika pierced his heart with a spear driven with speed.
From the heart of him who was split by the spear, another came forth, of great strength and great valour, a man saying, Stand.
As he was coming out, the Goddess laughed and then, roaring, cut off his head with her sword. Then he fell to the ground.
Then the lion devoured those asuras whose necks had been crushed by his fierce fangs, and Kali and Shivaduti devoured others.
Some great asuras perished, pierced by Kaumari's spear. Others were driven off by water purified by Brahmani's mantra.
Others fell, split by Maheshvari's trident. Some were crushed to powder on the ground by the blow of Varahi's snout.
Vaishnavi cut the danavas to pieces with her discus. Others were cut by the thunderbolt released from the tip of Aindri's hand.
Some asuras perished, and some fled from the great battle. Others were devoured by Kali, Shivaduti, and the lord of beasts.
